description:
Hazlewood Castle stands near Tadcaster in North Yorkshire, and its documented history reaches back to the 1086 Domesday Book, William the Conqueror's great survey of England compiled just two decades after the Norman Conquest. The Vavasour family's connection to the site dates from this Norman-era beginning: Mauger Le Vavasour, a vassal of the powerful William de Percy, took possession of the land after the displacement of the Saxon landholder Gamel, part of the wider redistribution that followed William the Conqueror's brutal 'harrying of the north' campaign of 1069–70, a scorched-earth suppression of Anglo-Saxon resistance in northern England that reshaped landholding across Yorkshire for generations.

What followed was one of the longest single-family tenures recorded at any English castle: the Vavasour family held Hazlewood continuously for more than 900 years, from that Norman-era beginning until 1908 — a span that dwarfs even the notably long tenures recorded at other properties in this collection, and places the Vavasours among a small handful of English families whose connection to a single estate persisted across nearly the entire span of documented English history since the Conquest.

Hazlewood's most historically significant chapter unfolded during the religious persecution that followed Henry VIII's break with Rome. As a Catholic family in a period when practising the old faith carried genuine legal danger, the Vavasours used their fortified house to shelter Catholic clergy, adding priest holes — concealed hiding spaces built into the tower specifically to hide priests during searches — along with an underground escape passage allowing clergy to flee undetected if the house was raided. The castle's own chapel, dating to 1286, considerably predates this Tudor-era persecution, giving Hazlewood a documented continuity of Catholic religious practice on the same site across more than seven centuries.

The Vavasour sale in 1908 opened a genuinely eclectic chapter in Hazlewood's later history. The building served as a maternity home, recording more than 2,500 births between 1939 and 1953 — a remarkable number for a single institution and a striking contrast to the castle's earlier defensive and religious functions. It later became a retreat for Carmelite friars, maintaining some continuity with the site's Catholic history even after leaving Vavasour ownership, and at one point served as the base for a celebrity chef, before finally opening as a hotel in 1997.

Today, Hazlewood offers genuinely strong evidence of public access on two distinct fronts. The Vavasour Restaurant & Bar welcomes non-residents daily for breakfast, lunch, afternoon tea and dinner, a comprehensive dining schedule matched by few comparable properties. Beyond dining, Hazlewood also runs real guided historical tours — not merely restaurant access dressed up as a visitor experience — on Tuesday, Wednesday, Friday and Saturday at 11am and 1pm, with advance booking required, taking visitors through the 1286 chapel and other historically significant areas of the building. This combination of confirmed daily dining access and a genuine, separately bookable guided tour product places Hazlewood among the more thoroughly documented public-access cases in this collection, comparable in spirit to Buittle Castle and Appleby Castle elsewhere in this pilot.

Hazlewood's setting also gives it a genuinely convenient position for visitors travelling between two of Yorkshire's most significant destinations: the city of York, with its own dense concentration of medieval and Roman history, lies within easy reach to the east, while Leeds and the wider West Yorkshire conurbation sit a short distance to the west. That geographic convenience, combined with the depth of the castle's own Vavasour family history and its unusually broad range of confirmed visitor access, makes Hazlewood a genuinely strong stop for anyone building an itinerary around this stretch of North Yorkshire.

faqs.question: Can I take a guided history tour of Hazlewood Castle?
faqs.answer: Yes. Hazlewood runs real guided historical tours on Tuesday, Wednesday, Friday and Saturday at 11am and 1pm, with advance booking required, taking visitors through the 1286 chapel and other historically significant areas — a genuinely separate visitor product from the hotel's dining offer.

faqs.question: What are 'priest holes,' and why does Hazlewood Castle have them?
faqs.answer: Priest holes are concealed hiding spaces built into a building specifically to hide Catholic priests from searches during periods of religious persecution. During the Tudor persecution of Catholics under Henry VIII, the Vavasour family, who were Catholic, added priest holes to Hazlewood's tower along with an underground escape passage, allowing clergy sheltering at the castle to hide or flee if the house was raided.

faqs.question: How long did the Vavasour family own Hazlewood Castle?
faqs.answer: The Vavasour family held Hazlewood Castle for more than 900 years, from the Norman era beginning with Mauger Le Vavasour until the estate was sold in 1908 — one of the longest single-family tenures recorded at any castle in England.

hotel.how_to_stay:
**Getting there:** near Tadcaster, North Yorkshire.

**Rooms & rates:** Only 9 of the property's 32 rooms are within the main castle building itself; the remaining 23 are split between the St Margarets annex in the Courtyard (12 rooms) and the separate St Leonard's building (11 rooms).

**On-site:** Vavasour Restaurant, real guided history tours (priest holes, 1286 chapel).

**Good to know:** If sleeping inside the 900-year Vavasour family's actual castle building is the priority, specify explicitly when booking — most of the hotel's rooms are in the two separate annex buildings.

**Combine with:** Leeds and York, both within easy driving distance.
